sentences.text: Tataouinea was an extinct sauropod dinosaur that lived in Tunisia during the Early Cretaceous period, specifically in what is now Africa during the Albian stage approximately 112 to 109 million years ago.
This animal was likely a relatively small, four-legged, herbivorous sauropod with a short neck, a long whip-like tail, and a light build.
It was the second-largest known member of the family Rebbachisauridae, after Limaysaurus tessonei.
Tataouinea had a notably wide snout with teeth only on the front of the jaw, resembling a vacuum cleaner.
The spinous processes of the sacral vertebrae fused to create a soft-tissue hump or sail, similar to Dicreosaurus.
The large neural processes of the vertebrae were shaped like an inverted Y.
The skull of Tataouinea was likely pneumatized through multiple holes, similar to Nigersaurus.
Nigersaurus taqueti was more than one-third smaller than Tataouinea hannibalis.
Until Tataouinea was discovered, similar structures had not been found in the ischial bones of other dinosaurs.
The presence of large pneumatic openings in the pelvic bones suggests a plausible internal ventilation system within the pelvic girdle.
The first elements of the holotype specimen were discovered in 2011 by Aldo Luigi Bacchetta, though excavation did not begin until 2012.
The fossil remains were studied by Federico Fanti, Andrea Cau, Mohsen Hassine, and Michela Contessi.
The genus name refers to the region of Tataouine where it was found, while the species name honors Hannibal, the Carthaginian military commander.
The holotype specimen, cataloged as ONM DT 1-36, consisted of pelvic bone fragments, several tail vertebrae, and sacral vertebrae.
The genus Tataouinea was named by Fanti et al. in 2013.
Only one fossil occurrence of Tataouinea has been recorded.
Tataouinea was quadrupedal because its front legs were shorter, causing its hips to rise above its hips.
Its extremely long tail was likely used as a weapon, similar to other Diplodocus-related dinosaurs.
As herbivores, Tataouinea fed on common gymnosperms of the time, including conifers.
Tataouinea likely ate low plants to avoid competition with large titanosaurs adapted to high-growing foliage.
Tataouinea's tooth shape indicated it simply plucked vegetation without chewing it.
Like other sauropods, Tataouinea likely swallowed small stones called gastrolites to grind unchewed plant material for digestion.
Vertebral morphology indicates Tataouinea was a rebbachisaurid closely related to European nigersaurines.
In its 2013 description, Fanti and colleagues placed Tataouinea in the subfamily Nigersaurinae of the family Rebbachisauridae.
Together with its sister group Limaysaurinae, Nigersaurinae forms the clade Khebbashia.
The parent group of Tataouinea is Rebbachisaurinae.
Tataouinea belongs to the family Rebbachisauridae.
Tataouinea fossils were found in the Jebel El Mra or Oum ed Diab members of the Aptian-Albian Aïn el Guettar Formation.
Known Tataouinea fossils were found in the Ain el-Gutter Formation near Oum ed-Diab, dating to the Early Albian.
Evidence shows Rebbachisauridae members existed simultaneously on both sides of the Tethys Ocean.
Tataouinea lived from 113.2 to 100.5 million years ago during the Albian stage.
It is noted that the pneumatization of Rebbachisauridae skeletons developed gradually, becoming more pronounced in the Rebbachisaurinae subfamily.
